title: Introduction to REST API Concepts
description: Understand the foundational concepts behind REST APIs before building them in ASP.NET Core.

data.text: **API** stands for **Application Programming Interface**. Think of it as a contract between two pieces of software: one application offers services, and another application consumes them. Every time your weather app fetches today's forecast, or your email client checks for new messages, an API is working behind the scenes.

data.title: Everyday APIs
data.text: Payment gateways, mapping services, weather data, stock prices, and identity providers (like Google Sign-In) are all accessed through APIs. You use dozens of APIs every day without seeing them.

APIs follow a simple **client-server** pattern. The **client** is the application that makes a request — for example, a web browser running JavaScript or a mobile app. The **server** is the application that receives the request, processes it, and sends back a response.

data.caption: How a client sends an HTTP request to a server and receives a response.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client (Browser / App)
  participant S as Server (Web API)
  C->>S: HTTP Request (method + URL + body)
  S-->>S: Process request
  S-->>C: HTTP Response (status + body)

data.text: What Makes an API a Web API?

A **Web API** is simply an API that is reachable over the internet using standard **HTTP** protocols. Because HTTP is universal, any technology — JavaScript, Python, Java, ASP.NET Core, or even PowerShell — can call a Web API.

data.title: Common Web API examples
items: OpenWeatherMap — returns current weather data for any city.
Stripe — processes payments and returns transaction status.
GitHub REST API — lets tools read and write repository data.
ASP.NET Core Web API — serves JSON data from your own backend.

data.text: Web APIs use standard HTTP request methods — called **verbs** — to describe the action the client wants to perform. The four most important verbs map directly to database **CRUD** operations.
**REST** stands for **REpresentational State Transfer**. It is an architectural style — not a protocol — that gives a set of rules for building Web APIs. A RESTful API follows these core principles:

data.title: REST principles at a glance
items: **Stateless** — every request contains all the information the server needs. The server does not store client session state between requests.
**Resource-based URLs** — data is addressed as a noun (e.g. /api/Reservation), not a verb (e.g. /getReservation).
**Standard HTTP verbs** — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE describe the action.
**Standard representations** — data is sent as JSON or XML with a matching Content-Type header.
**Uniform interface** — the same URL structure and conventions are used across the entire API.

data.caption: How REST maps CRUD operations to URLs and HTTP verbs.
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Client] -->|GET /api/Reservation| B[List all reservations]
    A -->|GET /api/Reservation/1| C[Get reservation #1]
    A -->|POST /api/Reservation| D[Create reservation]
    A -->|PUT /api/Reservation| E[Update reservation]
    A -->|PATCH /api/Reservation/1| F[Partially update #1]
    A -->|DELETE /api/Reservation/1| G[Delete reservation #1]
    style B fill:#4ade80
    style C fill:#4ade80
    style D fill:#60a5fa
    style E fill:#fbbf24
    style F fill:#fbbf24
    style G fill:#f87171

data.text: Every HTTP response includes a three-digit **status code** that tells the client what happened. Grouped by their first digit, the most relevant codes for API developers are:

rows: The request succeeded but there is no content to return (common after DELETE).
The request was malformed or invalid.
Authentication is required or has failed.
The requested resource was not found.
An unexpected error occurred on the server.

data.text: JSON — The Language of Web APIs
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is the most common format for exchanging data with Web APIs. It is human-readable, lightweight, and supported by every modern programming language.

terms.definition: A unique URL that a Web API exposes for a specific action, e.g. /api/Reservation.
The actual data carried in the body of an HTTP request or response.
The application that initiates an HTTP request to a Web API.
The application that receives HTTP requests and returns responses.
An operation that produces the same result no matter how many times it is called. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

data.description: Imagine you are building a Web API for a book library. Write the correct RESTful URLs for the following operations:
steps: Get a single book by its ID.
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce URLs like /api/Book, /api/Book/5, etc., paired with the correct HTTP verb for each operation.

items.text: I can explain the difference between a client and a server.
items.hint: The client makes requests; the server responds.

items.text: I know which HTTP verb to use for each CRUD operation.
items.hint: GET = read, POST = create, PUT/PATCH = update, DELETE = delete.

items.text: I understand what REST stands for and its core principles.
items.hint: REpresentational State Transfer — stateless, resource-based, uniform.

items.text: I can read a JSON response and identify the key fields.
items.hint: Look for id, name, and any domain-specific properties.
